# Ruchira Rajapaksha

> AI Product Engineer at Arbitr, Auckland. 7 years. Open work rights in New Zealand, no sponsorship needed.

Portfolio: https://lordmaduz.github.io/ruchira.codes/

## Roles

- AI Product Engineer, Arbitr (formerly Straker), Auckland (June 2026 to now): Orchestration, guardrails and human review around the AI agents on an AI-first translation platform, across Python services and Vue web apps.
- Founder & Engineer, LandedNZ (February 2026 to now): A web app that plans a move to New Zealand. A rules engine builds the plan and an AI chat answers questions about it. Now rebuilding it so every claim links to an official source.
- Senior Software Engineer, DBS Bank, Singapore (June 2024 to May 2026): Led design on a global minimum tax engine and on HAWK, a multi-agent hedge accounting workbench, plus high-volume Kafka services.
- Senior Application Developer, DBS Bank, Singapore (September 2022 to April 2024): Reactive trade file processing, an attribute-based access control engine at the API gateway, and live config across 40+ service instances.
- Senior Software Engineer, GrubTech, Sri Lanka (April 2022 to September 2022): Order management for 500K+ food orders a day, with write-behind caching and tracing.
- Software Engineer, DirectFN, Sri Lanka (Until April 2022): Trading platforms on Akka actors, including algorithmic order execution and anti-money-laundering pattern detection.

## Education

- MSc Software Engineering, research in blockchain, University of Westminster, United Kingdom
- BSc Statistics and Operational Research, University of Peradeniya, Sri Lanka

- Reviewed about 35 of my teammates' pull requests.
- The plan covers 21 tasks across your first 90 days.
- 5 things shape the plan: visa, city, family, job and arrival date.
- The chat's answer starts streaming in under a second.
- Processing went from 5 days to 2 hours per country.
- Deployment cycles for tax rule changes dropped by 80% once rules moved out of code into the engine.
- One engine covers 15+ countries.

- Handles 50K+ trade files a month.

- The platform took 500K+ orders a day.

- HAWK's accuracy went from about 60% to 99.5% in production, with business rules checking every step the agents take.
- HAWK cut operational cost by about 60% in production.
- HAWK covers the bank's structural FX hedges, more than S$100B.
- Services at DBS handled 1M+ transactions a day at 12K requests a second.
- An access control engine built on Cedar at the API gateway covered 30+ services and cut unauthorised access attempts by 95%.
- Live config with Spring Cloud Config and Spring Cloud Bus across 40+ service instances ended config-related outages.
- Microservices uptime held at 99% across 40+ services once live config ended config-related outages.
- Team of 6 at DBS. I made the design calls, split and reviewed work, and coached 4 engineers.
- Team sizes: GrubTech 3, DirectFN 5, Arbitr NZ engineering 4.
- Built a multi-agent system for the GAIA benchmark that got 85% on 20 medium-level tasks.
- About 80 posts on Medium and 6 tutorials on Baeldung.
- Trading apps on Akka got 45% more throughput and 30% lower latency.
- MSc in Software Engineering from the University of Westminster, with research in blockchain.
- BSc in Statistics and Operational Research from the University of Peradeniya.
- Learned Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic and Vue 3 with Nuxt on the job at Arbitr.
- About 350 merged pull requests across pre-production and production branches, and about 1,500 unique commits, in roughly four and a half months.
- About 80k lines of tests at Arbitr.
- Wrote 271 design specs and implementation plans at Arbitr before building.
- Reactive Kafka pipelines on Project Reactor cut data processing from 48 hours to about 4.
- Redis caching with careful invalidation made queries 40% faster across services.
- Those services ran at 20ms latency with 99.9% uptime.
- Shared standards across 15+ services cut codebase issues by 30%.
- Rejoined DBS in June 2024 as a Senior Software Engineer and took the technical lead role on two products.
- HAWK has two modes: role-gated prompt templates for everyday work, and a free-form agent mode for unusual questions.
- Every HAWK agent action carries an audit trail, and anything that books a deal or posts to the ledger waits for a person to approve it.
- Built an order SDK in Android and Flutter versions, so any front end could fetch nearby orders and get live order updates.
- Incident fix time fell by 75% after tracing went in.
- Fixed performance bottlenecks that cut memory use by 60% on the trading platform.
- LandedNZ has a typed error hierarchy, a versioned prompt registry, and thin adapters around the Claude API and storage, all in one TypeScript monorepo.
- Wrote up the AWS SDK v2 getObjectAsBytes memory problem on Medium so other teams migrating would avoid it.
- I don't ship code I can't explain line by line, whether a person or an AI wrote it.
- I don't put AI on a critical path without a plain, deterministic path underneath it.
- Nothing goes to production without logs, metrics and a way to roll back.
- I only bring in a framework or tool when the problem needs it.
- I write the design first: the problem, the approach and how it can fail. Then build, then review for failure modes, rollback and the next reader.
- My Claude Code setup runs in phases: research, a plan checked by a validator agent against architecture rules I wrote, then build with tests enforced by hooks and a reviewer agent after each piece. A /learn step saves each correction so the next session starts smarter.
- Most teams still lean on prompt engineering and throw one generic agent at every kind of task. Then they either let the agent decide everything or keep a person watching every step. Both are old habits, and neither is efficient.
- Overrated: autonomous agent pipelines with fragile orchestration, and microservices as the default. Underrated: deterministic logic under AI features, so reliability is designed in.
- What I push back on: clever abstractions nobody can read, AI-generated code dropped into a PR without thought, tech picked because it sounds good, and building for scale you won't hit.
- After building the same agent across four frameworks: smolagents suits a manager handing work to specialists, LangGraph suits explicit state machines, LlamaIndex suits retrieval-heavy work, and the raw SDK is where you learn what the frameworks hide.
- Built SettleAgent on the raw Anthropic SDK with vector memory in ChromaDB, to see how agents work with no framework in the way.
- Hugging Face Agentic AI certificate, January 2026. AWS Certified Solutions Architect, Associate, valid to January 2028.
- Trading platform reliability and user experience improved by 80% after fixing critical performance bottlenecks.

## Stories

### Leading the tax engine

Tax rules were hard-coded, so every regulation change meant code, a release and a retest. The people who understand the rules are tax professionals, so I built an engine where they write the rules themselves, versioned so an audit can replay any quarter. When the regulator changed its rules twice mid-build, the engine took both with no redeploy.

### Getting three teams on the same page

Three teams, 15+ services, and each had its own way of logging, testing and handling errors. None of them reported to me. I started open weekly sessions on real problems in our code, moved my own service first so there was a working example, then sat with each team lead for an afternoon. Issues across the platform dropped 30% over two quarters, and the sessions kept going after I moved on.

### Bringing two new engineers up to speed

Two engineers joined within a few weeks of each other, one from Java and one from Node. I paired with each on a real first feature, end to end. For the Node engineer I used what they already knew about event loops as the bridge into reactive Java. Both shipped on their own within the first month, and the Node engineer's write-up became our onboarding guide.

### Rules in code or rules the tax team owns

A senior engineer wanted to keep tax rules in code with a fast deploy pipeline. I wrote a one-page comparison against three real changes already coming from the regulator. He raised the runtime cost, which was fair, so I came back with benchmarks. He came round, and later pushed the same pattern on other projects himself.

### The 25MB surprise

During the AWS SDK v2 migration I picked getObjectAsBytes because it looked like the clean replacement. Tests passed, then production ran out of memory. The method has a hidden 25MB cap, and our real files were bigger. We rolled back in about ten minutes with no data lost. I moved to streaming, added a test file sized like production, and wrote it up on Medium so other teams wouldn't hit the same wall.

### When the regulator changed the structure

About three weeks before a milestone, the regulator changed the structure of the rules, which meant engineering work on our side. I ran it in two streams: we reworked the structure and the editor while the tax team checked which of their rules had to change. We froze anything non-essential and ran old and new formats side by side. We still finished 3 months before the FY2025 deadline, with a clean audit trail.

### A service split I undid

At DBS I split notifications and audit into two services because I thought they'd scale separately. Two months in it was clearly wrong: duplicated code, two pipelines on the same events, network calls where a function call used to be. I merged them back in about two weeks. My rule now: if you're not sure, keep it together and split when there's a concrete reason.

### Loud failures over silent ones

On HAWK the agent was grounded by a rules library that wasn't finished, and we had a ship date. The question was what happens when no rule matches. I pushed for a hard reject that says why, instead of letting the agent guess on something with financial outcomes. The compliance lead backed it straight away. The 'rule not found' count became the rules team's priority list.

### Building something I'd be woken up for

At GrubTech the same few engineers built the order service and took the on-call pages. So I added distributed tracing from day one, built dashboards around what diners actually see, and wrote runbooks while the design was fresh. Time to spot an incident went from 45 minutes to 9, and fixes got 75% faster.

### Two afternoons watching the tax team

The brief said 'Excel-like UI' and I wanted a form builder. I spent two afternoons watching the tax team work instead. They lived in worksheets: jumping between cells, tracing formulas back. So we built a sheet with named cells and formulas that compiled to rules underneath, and the tax team ran the design reviews. Alignment on a rule change went from 6 weeks to 2.

### A guardrail that didn't touch the agent

A new product's first clients needed only approved vendors picked by the AI vendor-selection agent. Instead of changing the agent, the workflow service filters its top 15 picks and sends the job to a person if none qualify. A project manager can override it, with the reason logged. It went live for the product's first client jobs.

### An agent that fixes client terms

Clients register exact terms, and machine translation didn't always use them. I designed an LLM repair agent that runs after the other agents, puts the exact term in and fixes the grammar around it. It's deterministic, it never trusts the model's own report of what it changed, and quality scoring waits until its repairs land.

### Filtering that hid jobs

The project dashboard filtered on a loaded page of 50 rows, so matching jobs on later pages never showed. I moved filtering, sorting and counts into one SQL query and skipped a schema change. When a reviewer worried about speed, I benchmarked it on real PostgreSQL: about 4.4x faster at 20k jobs.

### A 3-million-row clean-up

To remove duplicate glossary terms I added a normalised column, a batched backfill, a constraint and a search filter, across two repos. In pre-production it backfilled 3,007,543 rows in a little over 2 hours with no errors. When an early constraint crash-looped a container there, I traced it in the logs and reverted.

### Chasing vendors who never confirmed

Vendors who accepted an offer but never confirmed the order were never chased, and I found about 347 stale batches. I designed a sweep that reminds at 20% of the window, sends a final notice at 30%, then raises it for a person. A cross-model AI review caught a bug where the limit ran before the due filter, which could starve the sweep.

### Client complaints, end to end

Client complaints lived outside the system with no audit trail. I built the workflow across 4 services: tables, a state machine, an event log that can't be edited, and pushes to the operations console and vendor defect tracking that don't block the main save. After UX feedback the picker became a modal.

### Explaining automated vendor choices

To support EU AI Act transparency, I added an insert-only record of how each vendor was chosen, covering all 4 ways a vendor gets picked, plus a 'selection details' view. In review we made sure it keeps no personal data and clears stale agent evidence when it falls back.

### Testing a translation option before adopting it

I built an offline, repeatable benchmark for an adaptive machine translation option: 16 language pairs, 100 segments each, scored by the in-house quality model. It found a small but statistically significant drop for English into other languages, before anyone decided to adopt it.

### Which steps run automated and which go to people

The platform only knew whether a whole job was meant to be automated, so after a step moved on it couldn't tell which stages should still be automatic. I tested two designs. One failed a test because it would undo a manager's switch to manual; the other had a hidden bug a proof test found, which I fixed with a guard. I also built the exception console the agents raise work into, and an early warning before offers expire.

### Access control at the gateway

We had 30+ services in a zero-trust setup and no consistent way to check attributes at the gateway. I built a standalone policy engine on Cedar, inside the gateway process. Unauthorised access attempts dropped 95%, and it became the pattern for new services.

### Config changes without restarts

Any config change across our 40+ service instances meant a restart, and restarts at a bank aren't free. I set up Spring Cloud Config Server with Spring Cloud Bus so changes reach every instance live. Config-related outages stopped.

### Agents with rules underneath

HAWK started as a broad brief: bring the hedge accounting lifecycle, spread across teams and manual steps, into one platform using AI. I chose agents over a fixed workflow because the rules kept changing and people asked one-off questions. A proxy agent screens requests, an orchestrator splits the work, and specialist agents handle allocation, booking and posting. The business rules live in a knowledge base the model can't override, and a person approves anything with real side effects.

### Algorithmic trading on Akka

At DirectFN the main project was Athena, an order management system that lets insurance and hedge funds split large orders over time with algorithms like TWAP and VWAP so they don't move the market. Each algorithm ran as its own Akka actor with its own state and supervision. Tuning mailboxes, dispatchers and serialisation gave 45% more throughput and 30% lower latency.

### Spotting suspicious trades

I also worked on an anti-money-laundering engine that looks for suspicious trading patterns across several sliding time windows at once, without keeping every transaction in memory. It ran on typed Akka actors and Akka HTTP.

### One benchmark, four frameworks

Before moving into AI work full time, I spent about five months building the same kind of agent system in smolagents, LangGraph, LlamaIndex and the raw Anthropic SDK, against the GAIA benchmark. The smolagents version, a manager with research and audio/video specialists, got 85% on 20 medium tasks. I wanted my own view of which framework fits which problem.

## Decisions

- Before a new AI translation product took its first client jobs, how do we make sure its AI agent only picks approved vendors?
  - What I did: Filtered the agent's top 15 picks in our workflow service, keeping only approved vendors.
  - Instead of: Changing the agent itself.
  - Why: Other products use the same agent and rely on how it works today. If none of the 15 qualified, the job went to a person to assign.
- Clients register terms that must appear exactly in their translations. After the AI repairs a translation, how do we record which of those terms it used?
  - What I did: Checked the repaired text itself to see which terms are there.
  - Instead of: Taking the model's own report of what it changed.
  - Why: That record is the client's proof that their terms were followed. It shouldn't depend on a model describing its own work.
- The repair agent needs each client's glossary of required terms. How does it get them?
  - What I did: Sent the client's glossary along with each job.
  - Instead of: Calling the terminology service to look up terms for every segment (one sentence of the document).
  - Why: That call took about 7.3 seconds per 500 segments against a 5 second timeout, and it had already killed whole batches.
- LandedNZ gives people moving to New Zealand a step-by-step plan for settling in: bank account, IRD number, tenancy and so on. What should build that plan?
  - What I did: A rules engine that orders the steps for the person's situation.
  - Instead of: Letting the AI write the plan.
  - Why: A wrong step costs people real time and money. The AI answers questions about the plan but can't change it, so the plan still works when the AI is down.
- The AI assistant searches LandedNZ's own content before it answers. Where should that search data live?
  - What I did: In the main PostgreSQL database, using the pgvector extension.
  - Instead of: A separate database just for AI search.
  - Why: The data is small. One database means one backup and one thing to run.
- The GloBE tax rules covered 15+ countries and kept changing. Every change meant a code change, a release and a retest. How do we keep up?
  - What I did: Moved the rules into templates (written in MVEL) that the tax team edits themselves.
  - Instead of: Keeping the rules in code and speeding up releases.
  - Why: The rules changed too often for a release cycle, and benchmarks showed the templates ran fast enough for our volume.
- Auditors ask what the tax rules were on a given date. How do we answer exactly?
  - What I did: Gave every rule template a version number and kept the old versions.
  - Instead of: Editing rules in place.
  - Why: We can rerun any calculation against the exact version of the rules that applied on that date.
- Tax professionals, not engineers, write the rules. What should the rule editor look like?
  - What I did: A worksheet-style editor with named cells and formulas.
  - Instead of: A form builder, which was my first idea.
  - Why: I spent two afternoons watching the tax team work. They think in cells and formulas, and a form would have fought them at every step.
- After an SDK upgrade, the file service started running out of memory in production on large files. How should it read files from S3?
  - What I did: Streamed each file through in pieces.
  - Instead of: Loading each whole file into memory.
  - Why: The method we first used, getObjectAsBytes, has a hidden 25MB cap, and real trade files are bigger.
- Moving to Java 17 meant moving to version 2 of the AWS SDK. How should the file service call S3?
  - What I did: Used the reactive version of the SDK with WebFlux.
  - Instead of: Keeping blocking calls.
  - Why: We had to move to v2 anyway, and the blocking calls were the part that slowed down when markets got busy.
- At lunch peaks, MongoDB couldn't keep up with incoming orders. How do we keep orders fast?
  - What I did: Confirmed orders from a Redis cache and wrote them to MongoDB shortly after (write-behind caching).
  - Instead of: Writing every order straight to MongoDB.
  - Why: The database was the bottleneck at peak times. The cache takes the burst, and the writes catch up a moment later.
- I was on call for the order service myself. What should its dashboards track?
  - What I did: What diners see, such as how long a kitchen update takes to reach the diner's screen.
  - Instead of: Only the service's internal metrics.
  - Why: The diner's screen is where problems show first, and I wanted to find the cause from one dashboard when paged at 3am.
- I build LandedNZ alone, with a web app and an API. How should the code be organised?
  - What I did: One TypeScript repository for both, sharing the same types.
  - Instead of: Separate repositories for the web app and the API.
  - Why: Both sides use the same type definitions, so the API and the app can't quietly drift apart.
- 30+ services needed the same access checks at the API gateway. Where should the policy check run?
  - What I did: Inside the gateway, using Cedar.
  - Instead of: OPA running as a separate service.
  - Why: The check runs in the same process on the JVM, and Cedar policies have a formally defined meaning. We didn't have to run another service or learn another policy language.
- Changing config on our 40+ service instances meant restarting them. How do we push changes live?
  - What I did: Used Spring Cloud Bus with Spring Cloud Config.
  - Instead of: Our own Kafka topic for config updates.
  - Why: It was already part of our Spring stack, so we didn't have to run a second messaging setup.
- An order can get two updates seconds apart from different apps. How do we stop one wiping out the other?
  - What I did: Queued the changes at the service so they apply one at a time, in order.
  - Instead of: Letting the last write win.
  - Why: Otherwise one update silently overwrites the other, and the diner sees the wrong status.
- The hedge accounting assistant had to follow changing rules and answer one-off questions. How should it be built?
  - What I did: AI agents, with a rules engine underneath that checks their work.
  - Instead of: A fixed workflow graph.
  - Why: A fixed graph couldn't handle one-off questions or rules that kept changing. Every action that changes another system, like a booking, still needs a person to approve it.
- Some users wanted predictable steps, others wanted to ask anything. How should they work with the assistant?
  - What I did: Two modes side by side: ready-made templates and free-form questions.
  - Instead of: One free-form chat for everyone.
  - Why: Hedge professionals wanted predictable templates and traders wanted free-form questions. Offering both let each group start when they were ready.
- The agents had to work with several old bank systems. How should they connect?
  - What I did: Put an MCP-style adapter in front of each system.
  - Instead of: Wiring the agents straight to each system.
  - Why: The agents and the old systems can then change without breaking each other.
- Funds split large orders over time with trading algorithms like TWAP and VWAP. How do we run many of them at once safely?
  - What I did: Ran each algorithm as its own Akka actor.
  - Instead of: Shared state protected by locks.
  - Why: Each order had its own state and lifecycle. If one failed, it restarted on its own without taking the others down.
- When I started building AI agents, where should I begin?
  - What I did: Built on the raw SDK first.
  - Instead of: Starting with a framework.
  - Why: Frameworks hide complexity on purpose. I wanted to know what they hide before something breaks.

## How I work with AI

- I work in a fixed loop: a written spec signed off section by section, a plan checked against that spec, a git worktree per ticket, test-driven build, then review by several agents and by models from other vendors. Each correction becomes a written rule for the next session.
- For my own development and code review I use Claude Code plus a second AI coding harness behind the company's LLM gateway: 11 models from 5 vendors. I pick the model per task on cost, quality and speed.
- Cross-model review caught two critical bugs at Arbitr before merge: a background sweep that could skip work indefinitely, and a key collision when two events arrived in the same second.
- I use fresh agents with no prior context to audit specs and plans. I choose sequential or parallel agents per task, because fanning out is sometimes slower and costs more.
- I keep 33 workflow rules, each written after a mistake it now prevents.
- Token-compression tooling cut my token use by about 26% over 2,209 commands, and light work goes to cheaper models.
- I try new agent workflows on real tickets before recommending them. I ran a full epic on an alternative framework, wrote up the pros and cons, and that write-up informed the team's decision to stay with the current one.
- I use MCP integrations for the ticket tracker, ELK log search, and Playwright screenshots and layout checks.
- At Arbitr I adopted, extended and operationalised the team's AI tooling, and wrote a brand skill and guard tests that check later contributors' changes.
- I did about 35 AI-assisted peer reviews and helped 2 QA colleagues set up AI tooling.
- I moved from a Java stack to Python and Vue at Arbitr and made about 1,500 commits in four and a half months, using a spec-first, test-driven agent workflow with cross-model review on every change. That review caught two critical bugs before merge. I also evaluated two agent-workflow frameworks on live tickets, and my write-up informed the team's choice.
